paragraphs.text: A loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from Cangwu County in Guangxi, made in 1980. At forty-six years it is far past the decade after which the trade counts this tea as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged).

Like every [dark tea](dark:definition), its leaf is heaped after it is made so that warmth, moisture and microbes can darken it, and then it is packed away to age. Liu Bao was made for Chinese miners in Malaya, and most of it this old is [old stock](liu-bao:old-stock) that sat in warehouses after the tin mines declined. That is why the trade dates such tea by the basket, the labels and the papers packed with it.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
